projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The entire interview with Bob Obendorf was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div0.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of a videotaped interview with Bob Obendorf on behalf of the Veterans' Oral History Project. The interview is part of the Library of Congress collection of oral testimonies.
The interview was transcribed and processed byDiane Farrell.
The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus,
it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account.

To the extent possible, the spelling of places, names, foreign words, and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios, a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was your most favorite experience in the war?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: The Second World War, Korea, was going up at Thule Green and build an air base that because of the icebergs, they ran us out to sea and then back in. Icebergs are constantly moving and so we ran out. We had to weigh anchor and run out to sea and then come back and follow them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Cool. What was your least favorite experience?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Lisa, I cannot tell you of a bad experience.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really? What was your biggest surprise out of the whole war?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Put in the brig.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What's the brig?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Jail.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh. Why'd you get put in the brig?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Because I fell asleep at my gun.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And that is generally a court martial, because we were in a war. And I'd been up all day and all night.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And it was going into the next day, and it was just too long. And I told the fellows that were there to guard, because I was going to pull the gun up, lock it, and then sag and fall asleep for a little bit, which I did. Well, they got two hours and the lieutenant JG came along and shook me and said to me, are you asleep. I was asleep and yes, I woke up to the captain's mast. And in a captain's mast, they gave me ten days in the brig

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Were you there for all ten days?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes, out of sheer stupidity. Because when there was general quarters that sounded and we had to go to our gun positions, you could come out of the brig.
But I didn't come out.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Sheer stubbornness.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Trying to prove a point?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Trying to prove a point. And I was in there for ten days.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Wow. What did you fear the most out of the whole experience?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Japanese Zeros coming in with bombs and themselves. They were Kamikaze pilots.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you ever see any of them?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh, heavens, yes.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. We saw a battleship receive a torpedo from one of them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you know anybody on that ship?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And then he dive bombed into another one.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And that's their way of fighting.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you know anybody on any of those ships?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: No, okay. How old were you when you went into the war?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Almost 17.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was the typical age?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really? Wow. What was your -- the most life-changing experience in this whole thing?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: It would be I was chosen for -- because I took a test and they found out that I knew a lot about diesel. And at that time in my life, I didn't know what a diesel was, because I spent a lot of time on a farm.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So I was working my way through high school. I just happened to pass this test very well. And I got to go to the best diesel school in the world. And the other one was in Germany, where they invented diesel. I was picked out of there to be an engine man on board a submarine. And I kind of made a noise in line. And they took me right out. And so I was -- I was out of the submarine duty and back into the LST.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What does the engine room do on the submarine?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: They work on engines or piping, plumbing.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Or tanks.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, cool.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Or boat engines.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was your branch of service?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: United States Navy.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And what were your specific tasks in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: One task I had was they did not have a seaman that could run the captain's gig, which is the kind of fancy boat for the captain and the other officers.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And I could run it, I could steer, and control the men. So I -- I drove the boat.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And I took the commodore, captain, and other officers ashore and back. I had a very good job.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Good. What do you think people my age think about what you did for our country?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: At times, I think nothing. For instance, I looked through today in the paper and I saw people watching parades. And I saw the majority of the young people looking off into space or whatever or horsing around,
fighting, bumping one another, and so they didn't really understand what a parade was that was for war veterans, nor did they care. And that bothers me.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. How many leaves did you get while you were in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: How many what?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Leaves, like when you got leaves to go home.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh. I got -- when you come out of boot camp,
which is your initial training, you got a 30-day leave at that time. And it was wonderful. Well,
then when I was -- two and a half years while we were overseas, we came back for ship repair. And I got another 30-day leave, and that's all I got.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Two, that's all?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Two.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: How long were you in the war for?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I was in the war for -- I was in the war for six 20 years, but I was in the service for 12.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh. What was your favorite place that you went to?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: The Philippines. I would go back there today.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was so -- what did you like so much about the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: The people were so friendly. They were so inviting and so nice, that -- and I'm not saying they are today. I could well be surprised. But they're beautiful people, and I'm speaking of their skin.
It's kind of an olive color skin. And they're just -- they're all pretty well good-looking people.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I've heard that -- I've heard that from other people too.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: It's true. I'd go back there.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was your least favorite place you had to go?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I didn't have one.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really? Did you like all of them?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I liked them all. We went to -- we were in all of these invasions, and that's when the ship's, you know, right there on the shore.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And we anchored out, and we'd take supplies in by boat. I happened to be in the boat again and we made many a run to shore with soldiers. And that was quite exciting because generally when you drop the ramp to let them out -- submachine guns from the bushes; got 20 the first night.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. It was a scene.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you lose any of your friends in that?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Only one fellow was hit by -- he was across the ship and he was hit. A shell hit his barrel, came back and the shrapnel hit him, went through his life jacket.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And it scared him to death. Of course, we were all very young.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And he leaped out of -- he quit firing, leaped out of his gun and started to run. And I knew if he ran,

he was going to be in trouble, so I did the same thing and tackled him. And he went to Pearl Harbor or was taken to Pearl Harbor, and there he was treated and then later sent back. So I didn't lose anybody. But he was the only boy for a while. There wasn't anybody killed.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really? What was the worst thing that you saw happen there or any -- anyplace throughout your war time?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I was a part of it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What was it?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That was in Okinawa. And I didn't realize that that was such a terrible, terrible event, the invasion of 0kinawa. Lost some 55,000 people.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: When we were -- I was on an LST that goes up on the beach, opens the ramp doors, drops the ramp and then tanks, trucks, personnel would leave. We'd --
they'd exit the ship. The Japanese would -- had a --
had a dugout dug in the beach. And after these people hit, they jumped up out of the dugouts and were running towards us shooting. And we trained our guns down on them and we shot them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: All of them?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And that was terrible, terrible. That's the worst thing I did.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That's the worst thing. Well, we shot down five planes, but we didn't really see anyone. I saw one pilot but otherwise, these people I saw. That's a horrible thing.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. Wow. If you were doing an interview like this and you were my age, what's something that you would ask to the person you were interviewing?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: What could the person do, what could people do from the service to re-energize the youth to let them know how fortunate they are for what all the service personnel did to make the -- to save this country and to make the world a better world to live in by doing so.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay. And what do you think they could do? Go ahead and answer your own question there. That's a good one.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. I would like to -- I would like to see them,
some of them, if they could, be active with persons in the Navy, Army personnel. Like, I belong to a LST
club. I'd like to see some of them come there and listen and really see what happened and talk to some of the -- us old fellows. After all, we're in our s.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Is anyone in that LST club -- were any of them on the ship with you? Do you know any --

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No. Interesting story. I worked with a man five and a half years. And I talked about LST, the service, the war; nothing. We just didn't talk about it. We were both on an LST. We were both in the Pacific Theater of war and here we had worked together and -- and had never had any of these experiences go forward. But what was so interesting about that is the parts manager was in the service.
And one time our ship pulled alongside of his ship,

and I was leaning against the rail just kind of looking around. And he came up out of the engine room, quite sweaty and so forth because he was doing something down there that was very strenuous. And he was the parts manager of the store. And he and I worked, out and back and forth all the time. But this man never said anything, so we didn't know.
When I joined, there it is.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's weird. Now, are you guys really close?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Isn't that wonderful?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: We were very close then, and very close now.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's cool.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Isn't it?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That was a great experience.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: It really is. Wow. Now, you were in the Korean War also, right?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What were some of your experiences in the Korean War that you liked, the good -- are there really any good experiences or what you would consider a good experience?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, yeah, there are good experiences. Because you have to cross a time line --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- you have to cross the equator. And there's parties on board ship for those who do that.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And so you get a great big -- I mean, big certificate. And sometime when you're out, I'll show you.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: They're quite interesting, you'll be able to see.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That was interesting. Taking people ashore. And then I came back one time. We went back to Texas and got on a LSD, which is a landing ship dock. And we took workers from the government and shipping material for building bases, houses and -- and warehouses --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- as things for the Thule Green, up to the strait and see Eskimos.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do they really look like the stereotypical Eskimos that everybody thinks --

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: They look just like --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: -- with the parkas and fur?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Just -- just like that, only we had -- you know,
we went up there kind of in the summer.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And therefore, they didn't necessarily have the parkas on, but they had -- it was 14 below zero.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: In the summer?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Were you freezing?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Sometimes it would get to zero. And you know what? An amazing thing. You could go out -- I could go out like I'm dressed right now, short sleeves.
Now, don't touch metal, because if you touch it,
you're going to stick to it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: But you could go out in your short sleeves?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh, yes, went out -- oh, most of the time we were there.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Because the sun comes down, and it's very close and you're quite warm.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Cool. That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Isn't that amazing?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. I've never heard anything like that. What was the worst thing that you saw happen when you were in Korea in the war?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: The worst thing would be, back to what I said, in the Okinawa invasion. That was slaughtering people right on the beach.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. When you could actually see them face-to-face?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Face-to-face, running, and then all at once they weren't.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's horrible.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: It was horrible.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's horrible. What did you fear the most when you were in the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No. You're young then.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah. I guess it's more like a thrill than it would be --

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, it wasn't a thrill --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah, well --

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- because you had to work.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right. But it was -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: It was a -- it was a job. I'll put it that way.
So you did your job. We played cards. It was very warm. So when we were out waiting for boats to come take our produce and things ashore --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- we would -- and the deck would -- the water would come up through the ________________. So we dove off the railings and swam in the water with the sharks. Well, you see, that was the nice part about it. They pumped the water in through piping and big grates, like furnace grates.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And things like that. They couldn't get in.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So we were absolutely safe.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Fun.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That was fun. A nice little break from everything?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That, and when we had a lull in things we were doing, we would fish off the side.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you catch anything?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: A barracuda.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And a fish that has a -- like a ventilator on top of its head. It's approximately 30 inches long. And the ventilator's, oh, two inches wide and a foot long. And what -- they're scavenger fish. And what they do is hook themselves to the bottom of a shark.
And as the shark swims and he's eating, anything that comes by that he's not eating, scraps, hey --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And they get a free ride. I caught one of those and caught a baby shark.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah, about three feet long. We'd throw them all back in, except for the barracuda. We didn't throw him back in. We cut the chain, so he could go on. I don't know what ever happened to him.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you have any other favorite stories that you'd like to share?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah. When we went to Japan --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- we went ashore, some of us. And we always had a .45 and what they call a bolo knife, a big knife.
You'd take a swat at something, and you'd cut it in half.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh, yeah. A very sharp knife.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I'd be afraid of that.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: On one scythe. And so they told you not to go in the villages if you didn't have to because they didn't want any harm, they didn't want to cause any problems.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, I got near the edges of a village. Those people lived in huts on dirt. The only thing theyhad, carpet, rugs, that they'd roll out. You know,
you've seen them sitting around on those?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That's because they're living on dirt. And this way, they're not. So they would sit on it. And I went in many a hut. I'd say probably ten. One family give me a flag. The other one gave me saki.
And saki is a Japanese drink that is really potent.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And I -- you know, I didn't have that. And then I walked out of the village and over to the edge of a huge cliff there. Our ship was down in the bay.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And there was an old Japanese man sitting there on a white wrought iron bench smoking a pipe with ____________. And he was old. And I sat down beside him and tried to strike up a conversation.
Well, he didn't acknowledge that I was even there,
just kept puffing on his pipe. And finally I thought, I'm disturbing this person. And I left.
But I understood the whole situation that this man said we are invading his country.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And he didn't like it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And I don't blame him.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Exactly. I wouldn't either.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I wouldn't like it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-uh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And boy, he sure -- he didn't say a word. I liked that.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That was an experience.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yes. Do you have any others?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. This is bad.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Every day a Japanese tug would come alongside with a barge behind it. When I say alongside, that means that they pull up next to the ship. And then you'd dump the garbage over the side into the barge.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: They had what we called a one-lung diesel and that was (making noise). That's all the thing did, see.

But they could go along well. And it was very strong. We took it upon ourselves to dump the water hose in that exhaust pipe and turn the water on. And the thump, thump, thump, stopped. That was not good.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: But we did it.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you get yourself in a lot of trouble while you were over there?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I was very active. I was very active.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you wish to expound? You don't have to.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Oh, no, anything that -- I tried everything. For instance, the crane wasn't working well.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So even though I wasn't what they called on duty --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- I'd work on the crane, trying to make it work better --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- and things like that. I liked that. So I was always doing something.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Did you learn to speak any different languages --

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: -- while you were in any different places?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Very sad.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Do you wish you would have so that maybe you could have communicated with some of the other people if you were -- possibly like that Japanese man?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes, that would have been very interesting. But,
you know, again, I was working on a farm and going to school.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And I went out of school and signed up, you know.
They took me out of school for that --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- excuse me, put you aboard ship and away you go.
And so everything's an experience. You just don't have any one particular thing. Plus, you did things -- everything. On board ship there was always cliques.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: You had the cooks, the store clerks, the laundry people. They all -- they were above everybody.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, it was my goal to see if I could get in that and see what was ____________, and I did. When the cook would get up in the morning at four o'clock to light off the stoves --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- and they wouldn't light off for him, he'd come get me, say, come on out and light these things. So I'd go out and do that. Well, consequently, I got ice cream.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, a special treat?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yeah. A special treat.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Got to love that.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: You got to love it. I just wanted in that.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, that's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes, I had a good time in both wars. How I got into the Korean War, my brother was a reserve when he got out of the service, so every two weeks, on the weekend you had to do duty.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: He said, brother, why don't you come out and join up, and we'll be together in the service. And I said I like that.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So I went out and joined, and one month later I was drafted. I never saw him.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No. Four months later I was in the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: What made you go into the Navy as opposed to,
like, the Marines or the Army?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I never thought of anything else. I just thought the Navy would be marvellous on board ship, out in the ocean. And it was. The whales -- well, when ships are going along, porpoises --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- will go up alongside the ship and then they'll get in front of it. And then they'll stop, and the ship goes sliding right over. And what that does is the barnacles on the bottom of the ship --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- scratches their back.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So they'll do that for two or three hours.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh, that's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And also, there's flying fish, believe that or not.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I believe that.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. And you'd stand there at the railing and flying fish would come up. They'd fly maybe 30 feet,
and they're back in the water.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. But there's a whole bunch of them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: So there's various things to watch.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: A storm at sea. You can look over there and see a perfect black area --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- maybe 500 -- or not 500, 50 to 60 miles away,
and that's a rainstorm.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That was -- yes.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat. That's really neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: We got to see a lot.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Cool. Any other stories or are you out of them?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: No. At Leyte in an invasion, one of our -- oh,
boy what was that? I don't know. I don't know.
We'll say early invasions. I don't know whether it was one, two or three, for instance, because it's been too long ago.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: In fact, I'm surprised I'm remembering all this.
I got off the ship with another friend of mine --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: -- and we went ashore into a village that was near where we had run up on the beach, and the boat with the rail off the side. And my friend and I took this boat that was there. And these guys are jumping up and down and yelling and hollering. But they didn't bother us. They were just jumping (making noise).
And we didn't pay any attention to them. And up the river we went for a little bit. And we came back.
And the problem was they were trying to tell us that there were Japanese up there, and they didn't want us to get killed.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: How about that?

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's neat that they were watching out for you.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes, really.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Of course, it's too bad you guys didn't mind them.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, we didn't know what was going on.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yes, I know. I know.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Bleeble, bleeble, bleeble, whatever language they used. And in this same time, there was a money shortage for the key notes. There were also like an army.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And they'd go kill Japs and tell you where they were and all of this. And so in order to have money for them, the government, on a regular old -- and I don't know what that is anymore. But they'd grind out this ink thing, paper and blue ink.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. And it was actually good currency. And they used it for spending, buying groceries and so forth.
And I got a couple of those. That was very interesting.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Neat.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: I don't know what they call them, the machine.
They use to use them in schools, a form of a printer,
but I can't remember the name of them.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yeah, that's okay. That's neat that they did that.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: It was very interesting. I would never, never stop anybody from going in the service. As a matter of fact, when we came out, we had to sign a paper whether or not we thought persons that graduated from high school should go in the service.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Why did you say?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I have a lot of friends that went into the service after they graduated last year.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Now, while you were in the service, you could get an education.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: You could go to college.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And they would pay for it.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And they don't know.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yes. That's -- that's the bad part about that.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: That's why -- sadly enough, that's why a lot of people go into the service because they can't afford to pay for college, so they go in there so they can get expenses, but they're also helping their country.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Well, they're also helping their country, and they're -- they're generally people that aren't ready to go to work and they don't know what work is until they get in the service.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right. Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And some of their folks might call them kooks, because they don't know what they want to do.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: That, they don't mind for a while.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And then they want --

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: And they want?

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: And then they want to tell someone what to do.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Very interesting.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, thank you for letting me do this interview.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: You're very welcome.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: I learned a lot, and it was fun.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Very interesting. I don't know how I remembered some of it. It's way back.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Sometimes you just start talking, and it all just comes back.

sp.speaker: Bob Obendorf
sp.p: Yes. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Interviewer
sp.p: Well, thank you.
